title: S3 Compatibility Doesn't Guarantee S3-Level Security
gist: A Wiz study of S3-compatible object storage across six neoclouds (Nebius, Crusoe, Vultr, Lambda Labs, Cloudflare R2, DigitalOcean) found significant, inconsistent security gaps versus Amazon S3 — from missing public-access controls and undetectable credential formats to a bug where deleting a bucket policy on one provider deleted the entire bucket — arguing S3 API compatibility creates a false sense of portable security.

insights.claim: Wiz principal cloud security researcher Scott Piper argues S3 API compatibility creates a dangerous false sense of security portability: with nearly 300 APIs across AWS S3 and related services (S3 Tables, S3 Vectors, S3 Express) built up over 20+ years, most S3-compatible clones have not replicated the full functionality, and some behave in unexpected ways precisely where teams assume AWS-equivalent behavior.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Organizations treating S3-compatible neoclouds as drop-in replacements should explicitly re-verify security assumptions rather than assuming API compatibility implies protection parity.
insights.quote: There are nearly 300 APIs associated with AWS S3 and its related services (such as S3 tables, S3 vectors, S3 express, and more). All sorts of specialized functionality has been added to S3 over the more than 20 years of its existence, with trillions of objects and hundreds of exabytes of data stored within it. As you should expect, not all of that functionality has been replicated, and some of these S3 clones work in unexpected ways.
insights.locator: Piper argues S3 compatibility creates a dangerous false sense of portability

insights.claim: IAM capabilities and semantics differ considerably among S3-compatible implementations, a gap that has already surfaced as real vulnerabilities: one in MinIO enabled unauthorized privilege escalation, and a recent one in RustFS broke tenant isolation and authorization semantics entirely.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Confirms the portability-risk thesis with concrete, named CVE-class incidents (MinIO privilege escalation, RustFS tenant-isolation break), giving security teams specific products to prioritize in review.
insights.locator: IAM capabilities and semantics differ considerably among S3-compatible implementations

themes.theme: Concrete security gaps found across providers

insights.claim: Public-bucket handling varies significantly across the six neoclouds tested: Crusoe and Lambda Labs lack public-access capability entirely; Nebius and Cloudflare R2 allow public buckets but not anonymous object listing; DigitalOcean supports publicly listable buckets; and Vultr supports both ACLs and bucket policies for public access — a spread of protection levels far wider than AWS S3's Block Public Access default.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A concrete per-provider risk matrix for public-bucket exposure — teams choosing among these six neoclouds should treat public-access control as a differentiating, not assumed, capability.
insights.locator: S3-compatible services vary significantly in how they handle public buckets

insights.claim: S3-compatible services often lack the structured access-key formats and secret-scanning support that AWS credentials have, making leaked credentials for these services harder for both security teams and tools like GitHub's secret scanning to detect, in part because some providers' key formats have no scannable pattern.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Leaked-credential detection tooling that teams rely on for AWS keys may silently fail to catch equivalent leaks for these S3-compatible providers, a blind spot worth explicitly testing.
insights.quote: There are other credentials detected by GitHub for DigitalOcean and Cloudflare through GitHub's secret scanning process, but not these. These credentials for the S3 compatible services are also not commonly found by other secret scanners. Part of the reason is that some of these do not have patterns that can be used.

insights.claim: Corey Quinn of The Duckbill Group highlights a specific found bug: on one of the tested neoclouds, calling the delete-bucket-policy API deleted the entire bucket rather than just removing its policy.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A striking concrete example of API-behavior divergence that could cause accidental, irreversible data loss for teams assuming standard AWS S3 API semantics apply uniformly across clones.
insights.quote: Every neocloud ships an S3-compatible endpoint, and your muscle memory follows you there whether the APIs behave or not. Wiz went poking through Nebius, Crusoe, Vultr and friends in this look at the S3 clones. On one, `delete-bucket-policy` deleted the entire bucket. Worth reading before you assume Block Public Access exists.
insights.locator: Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at The Duckbill Group, summarizes it in his newsletter

themes.theme: Universal shared risks and defensive guidance

insights.claim: Because all the S3-compatible clones inherit presigned URLs from the S3 API, every one of the six tested providers supports this capability and carries its associated security implications, meaning presigned-URL risk is a shared, universal exposure across the S3-compatible ecosystem rather than an AWS-specific concern.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Presigned-URL misconfiguration risk should be audited on every S3-compatible provider a team uses, not assumed to be an AWS-only concern already covered by existing AWS-focused controls.
insights.locator: As S3-compatible services inherit presigned URLs from the S3 API

insights.claim: Wiz senior solutions engineer Rishi Raj Singh's core recommendation for teams using S3-compatible neocloud storage is to explicitly audit API behavior, verify permissions models, and validate what happens when standard AWS tooling interacts with these endpoints, rather than trusting default assumptions.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A direct, actionable checklist item for security teams: treat AWS-tooling behavior against non-AWS S3-compatible endpoints as untested until explicitly validated.
insights.quote: If you are leveraging S3-compatible storage in neoclouds, ensure your team is explicitly auditing API behavior, verifying permissions models, and validating what happens when standard AWS tooling interacts with these endpoints.
insights.locator: Rishi Raj Singh, senior solutions engineer at Wiz, writes on LinkedIn

insights.claim: Wiz's review covers only six neoclouds and explicitly does not include several other major S3-compatible implementations such as Backblaze B2, Wasabi, and Google Cloud Storage, even as the broader market has grown to more than 90 listed S3-compatible providers.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: The study's findings should not be assumed to generalize to unreviewed providers like Backblaze B2, Wasabi, or Google Cloud Storage, which may have materially different security postures.
insights.locator: Wiz’s review does not cover several other major S3-compatible implementations
